meta.title: Who really said "Tomorrow is another day"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Scarlett O'Hara's closing line is "After all, tomorrow is another day" — and Margaret Mitchell wrote it for the 1936 novel, not the 1939 film.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Tomorrow is another day'?
meta.ogDescription: The real line keeps "After all." Margaret Mitchell wrote it as her novel's last line in 1936 — and the proverb inside it was in print by 1600.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “After all, tomorrow is another day!”
answer.sourceLine: The sentence closes Margaret Mitchell’s novel Gone with the Wind (Macmillan, 30 June 1936), chapter 63: “After all, tomorrow is another day.” The 1939 film gives Scarlett the line essentially verbatim — the popular version simply drops Mitchell’s “After all,” which is the half of it that she actually wrote. The proverb inside it is anonymous and was already in print by 1600.
answer.confidenceText: The film didn’t originate the line, and neither did Mitchell coin the proverb — but the famous sentence is hers.

source.heading: The closing page of the novel

docMeta.dd: Gone with the Wind, pt. 5, ch. 63 — the novel’s final line
Scarlett O’Hara (Vivien Leigh) — a fictional character; screenplay credited solely to Sidney Howard, who did not write this sentence
The proverb “To-morrow is another day” appears in England’s Helicon (1600), signed “Ignoto”

source.excerpt:
With the spirit of her people who would not know defeat, even when it stared them in the face, she raised her chin. She could get Rhett back. She knew she could. There had never been a man she couldn’t get, once she set her mind upon him.

“I’ll think of it all tomorrow, at Tara. I can stand it then. Tomorrow, I’ll think of some way to get him back. After all, tomorrow is another day.”
trail: The film line, from a transcription, not memory. Wikiquote’s page for the 1939 film ↗ transcribes Scarlett’s speech ending “After all…tomorrow…is another day!” and heads the page “Written by Sidney Howard, based on the novel by Margaret Mitchell.” AFI independently lists it at #31 ↗ as “After all, tomorrow is another day!” Both keep “After all”; the popular quotation does not.

The novel outranks the film. The complete 1936 text at Project Gutenberg Australia ↗ ends: “Tomorrow, I’ll think of some way to get him back. After all, tomorrow is another day.” The film’s version is that sentence, unaltered — so the screenplay cannot be its origin, whoever held the credit.

Mitchell didn’t coin the saying. Wiktionary treats it as an English proverb ↗ and cites a 1600 use of unknown authorship. That citation checks out against the scan: in A. H. Bullen’s edition of England’s Helicon ↗, “Phyllida’s Love-call to her Corydon” reads “Remember, remember, / To-morrow is another day,” and closes “Finis. Ignoto.” Phrase Finder likewise states Mitchell did not coin it ↗, citing Harper’s Weekly in 1857.

The title clinches Mitchell’s authorship of the sentence. Wikipedia’s article on the novel ↗ records that Mitchell tentatively titled the book Tomorrow Is Another Day, “from its last line,” before choosing a phrase from Ernest Dowson’s “Cynara” — independent confirmation that the line was hers and on her final page three years before any film existed.
source.excerptNote: The last words of the novel. Searching the full text turns up the phrase exactly once in roughly 420,000 words — Mitchell spent the entire book getting to it. On screen, Scarlett reaches the same sentence via an added run-up (“Tara! Home. I’ll go home. And I’ll think of some way to get him back”), but the closing sentence itself is unchanged.

source.rightsNote: The sentence at issue first appeared in Gone with the Wind, published 30 June 1936 — well after the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, so it remains in copyright. Wikipedia notes the novel will not enter the US public domain until 1 January 2032 ↗. The bare proverb is ancient and unprotectable, and the 1600 England’s Helicon text is long public domain — but Mitchell’s sentence and the 1939 film are not. Note that the full text linked here is hosted by Project Gutenberg Australia, where the novel is public domain; it is not free to use in the United States.

author.name: Margaret Mitchell
author.kicker: The author of the real line
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Margaret Munnerlyn Mitchell was an Atlanta journalist who wrote one novel. Gone with the Wind, published by Macmillan on 30 June 1936, won the Pulitzer Prize and became one of the best-selling novels in American history; she resisted pressure to write a sequel until her death in 1949. She briefly considered titling the book “Tomorrow Is Another Day” — taken from its own last line, the very sentence at issue here.

Proverb attested earlier in England’s Helicon (London, 1600), “Phyllida’s Love-call to her Corydon, and his Replying,” signed “Ignoto.”

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody fabricated this one — the film is real, the character said it, and the sentence exists. But three different things get mixed up: who wrote the sentence, what the sentence is, and who coined the saying inside it.

items.why: The quoted form drops the opening. Wikiquote’s transcription of the film renders it “After all…tomorrow…is another day!”, and AFI lists quote #31 as “After all, tomorrow is another day!” ↗ The novel agrees: “After all, tomorrow is another day.” “After all” is the part Mitchell added to the proverb — it is the only part that is original, and it is the part that gets cut.

The line is commonly filed as a movie quote, but it is the last sentence of Mitchell’s 1936 novel, reproduced on screen without changes — the novel’s closing page ↗ reads “Tomorrow, I’ll think of some way to get him back. After all, tomorrow is another day.” Sidney Howard holds the sole screen credit for the screenplay, but this sentence is not his invention.

Scarlett is a fictional character and Vivien Leigh is the actor who performed the line; neither wrote it. Quote collections that credit “Scarlett O’Hara” as the author are crediting a person who does not exist.

The 1600 poem carrying “To-morrow is another day” is signed “Ignoto” — unknown. Its Victorian editor A. H. Bullen noted that the poem “has been ascribed, without the slightest authority, to Sir Walter Raleigh” ↗. This page names no poet, because the source does not.

misattribution.truthLine: Margaret Mitchell wrote “After all, tomorrow is another day” as the final line of Gone with the Wind in 1936; the 1939 film kept it word for word; and the proverb she built it from ↗ was already in print in 1600, by an author nobody knows.

context.heading: A proverb, a novel, then a film
lead: The phrase does three jobs at once, and the credit gets lost between them. As a proverb it is old, anonymous and unremarkable — a stock English consolation, in print by 1600 and still ordinary enough that a New York Times interviewee reached for it in 2005. As a sentence it is Margaret Mitchell’s: she put the old saying in Scarlett O’Hara’s mouth, prefaced it with “After all,” and made it the final beat of a 1,000-page novel. As a movie quote it is a transcription — the 1939 film simply kept what Mitchell wrote.

The word doing the work is the one people drop. “Tomorrow is another day” is a platitude. “After all, tomorrow is another day” is a character refusing to accept an ending — the shrug of a woman who has just lost Rhett Butler and has decided, in the space of a comma, not to think about it yet. Mitchell knew what she had: she nearly called the book Tomorrow Is Another Day, after its own last line, before settling on a phrase from an Ernest Dowson poem.
context.detailsSummary: How much of the film’s dialogue was actually written for the film?
detailsBody: Gone with the Wind’s screenplay is famously crowded: Sidney Howard’s draft was revised by Ben Hecht, Jo Swerling, Oliver H. P. Garrett, John Van Druten, Barbara Keon and producer David O. Selznick himself, though Howard received the sole screen credit ↗ and a posthumous Academy Award after dying in a farm-tractor accident before the premiere.

Selznick, in an October 1939 memo, described how little of the dialogue was invented: he claimed that of the material in the picture not drawn from the book, most was his own, with only a few original lines each from Howard, Hecht and Van Druten. The closing line was not among the inventions — it came straight off Mitchell’s last page. This is the same pattern as the film’s other famous exit line: Rhett’s “Frankly, my dear, I don’t give a damn” is in the novel too, as “My dear, I don’t give a damn.” There the film added a word. Here it added none.
context.pull: Mitchell wrote the sentence. She did not write the saying — that one is 336 years older, and signed “Ignoto.”
